opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not very reliable, and I don't think it's going to get much better. Detectors are trying to tell machine text from human text by statistical fingerprints, things like how predictable each next word is. But those fingerprints are fragile. Paraphrase the output, ask the model to write in a slightly different style, or have a person lightly edit it, and the signal largely goes away.

The deeper problem is that these systems are trained to imitate human writing. The better they get at that, the less there is to detect. So you're in an arms race where the generators have the structural advantage.

And the error rates matter a lot in practice. We've already seen students accused of cheating because a detector flagged their essay, and the false positives seem to fall disproportionately on non-native English speakers, whose prose can look more "predictable" to these tools. When you're making consequential decisions about someone's career or education, a tool that's right most of the time isn't good enough, especially when you don't know when it's wrong.

Watermarking is the more promising idea in principle, where the model subtly biases its word choices in a way you can check later. But it only works if the companies cooperate, it can still be degraded by paraphrasing, and open-source models simply won't include it. So it's a partial measure at best.

What worries me more is the bigger picture. We're heading toward a world where the cost of producing plausible-sounding misinformation is basically zero, and we don't have reliable technical tools to filter it. I think we need policy as well as technology: disclosure requirements, some accountability for the people deploying these systems at scale, and more investment in provenance, meaning authenticating what's real rather than trying to catch everything that's fake. Detection alone isn't going to save us.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not very reliable, and I think people need to stop pretending otherwise.

Look, the fundamental problem is that these systems are trained to produce text that's statistically indistinguishable from human text. That's the whole objective. So when you build a detector, you're essentially trying to find a signal that the generator was explicitly optimized to erase. That's a losing arms race by design. Every time the detectors get a little better, the next generation of models closes the gap, or someone just runs the output through a paraphraser and the signal evaporates.

And the empirical record bears this out. OpenAI released a classifier and then quietly pulled it because it wasn't working. The academic detectors, GPTZero, Turnitin, all of these things, have false positive rates that are genuinely alarming. There was that study showing non-native English speakers get flagged at much higher rates because their writing is more formulaic, more predictable, which is exactly the low-perplexity signature these tools key on. So you've got a tool that doesn't work well and is also biased in a way that hurts the people least able to defend themselves. That's a bad combination. Students have been accused of cheating based on these things, and in many cases the evidence is essentially noise.

Now, I want to be careful. There are narrow cases where detection is more tractable. If you have watermarking built into the generation process, cryptographically, at the token sampling level, that can work reasonably well, at least until someone paraphrases or mixes outputs. But that requires the model provider to cooperate, it requires that the model you're worried about is one of the watermarked ones, and open-weight models blow a hole right through it. So it's a partial solution to a problem that's inherently leaky.

The deeper point, and this is something I've been saying for a while, is that the industry made a choice to release these systems at scale with essentially no provenance infrastructure, and then told everyone else, teachers, journalists, platforms, that it was their problem to sort out. Detection is being asked to do a job it can't do, as a substitute for the governance that should have happened up front.

So my short answer is: treat any individual detection verdict with deep skepticism. At the population level you might see trends. At the level of "did this particular student write this particular essay," I wouldn't hang anything consequential on it.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t put a lot of confidence in it. You can build a detector that works reasonably well on a particular model under particular conditions, but that’s different from reliably identifying machine-generated text in the wild. Change the model, change the prompt, or have somebody edit the output, and the detector may fail.

And you have errors in both directions. You miss some machine-generated text, and you accuse people who actually wrote something themselves. If you’re using this to accuse a student of cheating, that second kind of error matters enormously. A detector’s score shouldn’t be treated as proof.

The underlying problem is that there isn’t some necessary signature of machine-generated language. These systems are designed to imitate human text. So I’d distinguish finding statistical clues from establishing who wrote something. The first is possible; the second is much harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical that we can do it reliably in the general case. You might build a detector that works reasonably well for a particular model under particular conditions, but that’s different from having a dependable test for whether something was written by a human or a machine. Change the model, change the prompt, or edit the output, and the detector may fail.

And false positives matter enormously. If you’re accusing a student of cheating, saying that a classifier thinks their essay looks machine-generated isn’t sufficient evidence. Fluent, predictable prose can come from a human, too. So I would treat these systems as providing a fallible signal, not a verdict.
